t: Number of Different Subsequences GCDs — Sieve Over Candidate GCD Values
o:
**Understanding the problem**

We inspect every non-empty subsequence of nums, take its GCD, and must report how many **distinct** GCD values occur. In Example 1 (nums = [6,10,3]) the three singletons give 6, 10 and 3; the pair [6,10] contributes 2; the whole array contributes 1 — five distinct values. Example 2 (nums = [5,15,40,5,6]) yields 7: the singletons 5, 15, 40, 6 plus gcd(40,6)=2, gcd(15,6)=3 and gcd(5,6)=1. With up to 10^5 elements, enumerating the 2^n subsequences is hopeless. The way out: every achievable GCD is at most max(nums) <= 2*10^5, and it must divide at least one element — so we enumerate candidate GCD **values** and test each one for achievability.
k: Appending elements never increases a subsequence GCD, so the strongest witness for candidate g is the set of ALL array values divisible by g.
Value g is achievable iff some element is divisible by g and the GCD of all elements divisible by g equals exactly g; otherwise that combined GCD overshoots to a larger multiple of g.
Iterating multiples of every candidate costs a harmonic series — about A*ln(A) visits for A = max(nums) — independent of n.

a.n: Approach 1: Grow the Set of Seen GCDs
a.i: Process elements left to right while keeping the set of GCDs realized by subsequences of the processed prefix. A new element x extends every existing subsequence (producing gcd(old, x)) and also forms its own singleton, so the updated set is the union of the old set, {x}, and all those combined values. This mirrors exactly how subsequences form and is easy to argue correct, but the set can grow explosively.
s: Initialize an empty set gs of achievable GCDs.
For each x in nums, build nxt = {x} union {gcd(g, x) for g in gs}.
a.t: O(n * |gs| * log V) — each element combines with every GCD seen so far, and |gs| can grow exponentially, so this times out on large inputs
a.sp: O(|gs|) for the set of achieved GCDs

a.n: Approach 2: Enumerate Candidates and Their Multiples
a.i: Flip the question: instead of asking which GCDs the array produces, test each value g for producibility. Record presence of every value in a boolean table. For candidate g, walk the multiples g, 2g, 3g, ... collecting the ones that occur and folding them into a running GCD. Because absorbing more elements can only lower a GCD, this running value is the minimum achievable GCD among subsequences drawn from multiples of g; the candidate succeeds exactly when it lands on g. An early exit triggers once the running GCD hits g.
s: Build a boolean present[] table over values up to A = max(nums).
For each g from 1 to A, scan multiples m = g, 2g, ... <= A and fold present ones into cur = gcd(cur, m).
Break the scan early once cur equals g.
Count g when cur == g; return the total count.
a.t: O(A log A + n) — the nested loops make about sum(A/g) = A*ln(A) visits, each an inexpensive gcd that the early exit usually cuts short

w:
**Wrap-up**

Mention the incremental-set idea to show command of the substructure, then pivot to the candidate sieve, which is the intended solution and comfortably fits the limits. Pitfalls: counting a value g merely because it divides some element (nums = [4,8] admits no GCD of 2 — the combined GCD of all even values is 4); forgetting that singleton subsequences make every distinct element achievable (the multiple m = g covers this automatically); scanning multiples without the early exit, which is noticeably slower in Python. The answer counts distinct values, not subsequences. Follow-up: for values up to 10^9 the sieve is impossible — enumerate divisors of each element (roughly a hundred per value) and run the same combined-GCD test over divisor groups.
